newsitem.title: UK: Tradepoint confident on future, doubts remain.
newsitem.headline: Tradepoint confident on future, doubts remain.

text.p: The Trade Point Investment Exchange, the main rival to the London Stock Exchange said on Wednesday it remained confident that it would secure long-term financing, enabling the fledgling share exchange to not only survive but to prosper.
But some market observers, including a few Tradepoint clients, fear Britain's first order-driven, electronic stock exchange's future is bleak.

Tradepoint managing director Michael Waller-Bridge dismisses suggestions that the days are numbered for the 20-month old exchange. He told Reuters the company on Wednesday had raised 775,000 stg in short-term working capital through a placing of 1.6 million new shares.
"You only have to look at the confidence that was shown in our placing today, which was oversubscribed," Waller-Bridge said.
"Our sources of long-term financing are quite wide."

Waller-Bridge said Tradepoint, which runs on an annual budget of around six million stg, had already raised about 21 million stg over the past two years but declined to give a figure on the amount of the long-term cash he hoped to secure.
"We're not publishing an exact figure but it will be in excess of one-year's operating budget, in other words more than six million pounds," he said.

On Monday, shares in Tradepoint, which offers investors a facility to buy and sell shares electronically in more than 900 British companies, plunged 25 percent on concern that the exchange, which is losing money each month, might be put into the hands of an administrator.
The share nosedive forced the company to announce an "interim financing arrangement" and a plan to secure long-term finance by the end of July.

While Waller-Bridge has no doubt that funds will be found and that Tradepoint will achieve its near-term goal of two percent of total London share turnover by year end, some of his clients are sceptical.
"I cannot think they will find enough money to keep going. A lot of money has already been put into the project," a senior executive of a British stockbroker said.

The broker, who wished to remain anonymous fears Tradepoint will eventually fold, even if it does secure lines of credit, due to competition from the LSE's own electronic system, which is set to launch in October.
"Events have overtaken them now that the(London)stock exchange has developed Sequence 6(electronic dealing system)," the broker said.
"The Sequence programme will overtake Tradepoint just before they reach critical mass. It has just taken them too long to develop their business."
Tradepoint must capture two percent of London share business in order to break even but Waller-Bridge admits that on a "good day" his exchange struggles to reach 0.5 percent.

Waller-Bridge said he was "looking forward" to the launch of the LSE electronic dealing system, which like Tradepoint, will match buyers and sellers directly through a computer terminal, cutting out the current LSE middlemen, or market makers.
"At the moment, Tradepoint is seen as a fringe exchange. Once the LSE starts its own system, we will jump from the fringe to the mainstream," Waller-Bridge said.
"The market will then see that our system is more cost effective. They will see the clear blue water that lies between us."
The head of trading at a major investment house, also a Tradepoint client thinks the clear blue water, however, will become a watery grave for Tradepoint.

"It's basically a good system and there is a need for it but given the choice of using the LSE's new system and Tradepoint's, I fear the market is going go with what it knows," the head of trading at a major investment house said.

"The tragedy is Tradepoint will become a victim of its own success. They really forced the LSE to finally switch to an order-driven system. I hope it survives but I think time has just about run out."
